title: Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason
full_review:
The trouble with some sequels is that the filmmaker often forgets what happened in the first movie, or assumes that the audience has forgotten.
Take, for example, the retread comedy "Bridget Jones: Edge of Reason" (Universal).

In it, Renee Zellweger reprises her role as the plump, romantically challenged Jones, who, though "a love pariah no more," finds herself navigating the same minefield of jealousies and insecurities that she supposedly overcame in the original.

"Edge of Reason," which picks up the action six weeks after "Bridget Jones' Diary" left off, opens with Jones literally turning a fresh page in her life, announcing through voice-over that she is starting "a new year and a new diary." It's a shame that all its entries are filled with recycled story lines and rehashed humor.

Colin Firth is back as Jones' dashing but stuffed-shirt boyfriend Mark Darcy. Having won his heart in the first go-round, Jones is now faced with the equally daunting challenge of holding on to it, a proposition which -- though seemingly a foregone conclusion at the end of the first film -- is made more precarious by the hovering presence of brainy and beautiful barrister Rebecca (Jacinda Barrett).

An embarrassing gaffe at a stuffy lawyers' banquet triggers a relapse of Jones' "singleton" self-loathing.
Her insecurities are further fanned by Darcy's noncommittal response when his parents prod him about his long-term intentions, a curious turn of events given the time and energy expended in the original trying to prove to us how much Darcy supposedly loved Jones.

Hugh Grant is also back as the caddish Daniel Cleaver, Jones' ex-boss and former lover. And though he has switched careers -- he now hosts a travel show for the same TV station for which Jones works -- his rapier wit and womanizing ways remain unchanged.

But then again, everything is pretty much unchanged, including the same farcical faux pas, slapstick sight gags involving Jones' ample derriere and invariable "shagging" references. There is even a carbon-copy scuffle between Darcy and Cleaver -- down to the comically choreographed fisticuffs -- only this one takes place in a fountain.
There are some minor novelties, but they're mostly scenic, including a ski trip to Switzerland and a ludicrous stint in a Thai prison by Jones after being wrongfully accused of drug smuggling. (She goes to Thailand on assignment for her TV show, along with Cleaver, who -- surprise, surprise -- tries to seduce her.)

Directed by Beeban Kidron, the film is buoyed by the bulls-eye performances of Zellweger, Firth and Grant, who are all at the top of their game. Zellweger, who once again packed on pounds for the role, is more ditzy and dumpy this time around, almost to the point of caricature, but still manages to fire off her self-deprecating zingers with endearing charm.

Unfortunately, one other thing that hasn't changed is the film's cavalier attitude toward premarital sex, which many viewers may find troubling. Still, underneath its bawdy bedroom humor is a theme that speaks to the wider human desire to be loved in spite of our imperfections -- what Jones would call our "wobbly bits."

"Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason" has its entertaining moments. But if you've seen the first movie, there isn't much "reason" to spend your time or money on this follow-up.

Because of several implied sexual encounters and a lesbian subplot, as well as an instance of rough language and recurring crude sexual language and humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
